en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One, the Jina, the peerless person, had risen from Rājagṛha and was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now, Ajātaśatru had a son, renowned by the name Siṃha.
Then, escorted by five hundred sons of guild-leaders,
he departed from Rājagṛha with great royal splendor;
taking a golden parasol, he approached the presence of the Buddha.
They gave parasols to that great seer;
having bowed their heads at his feet, they were all established in awakening.
With palms joined in reverence, Siṃha questioned that sage.
Tell me, as I ask you, what is that practice of the bodhisattvas?
By what means would one become pleasing to behold, and by what means would one be born spontaneously?
By what means would one remember one's past lives? Tell me this, O Great Sage!
Knowing their resolute intention through his wisdom, the Buddha said:
"I shall explain to you that practice of the bodhisattvas which you have asked about.
One should be serene through patience and be born spontaneously in the state of pure conduct."
"O young man, know this from the gift of Dharma that you possess the memory of your past lives.
How could he satisfy sentient beings with a body possessing the thirty-two marks and the secondary characteristics, like the descendant of Aṅgiras? [8–9]
The primary marks are attained through all forms of giving, and the secondary characteristics through loving-kindness;
by means of equanimity toward all sentient beings, one becomes a Jina of the lineage of Aṅgīrasa.
By what is the dhāraṇī obtained? By what is meditative concentration known?
And how does one become one whose speech is worthy of being accepted? Tell me that, O Great Sage.
For through the patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti) comes the dhāraṇī, and through the contemplation of meditative absorption (dhyāna) comes samādhi.
[Through] the patience regarding phenomena...
Through the cultivation of truthful speech, one’s words become authoritative.
By what means is one born possessed of mindfulness, and how does one become possessed of intelligence?
O Great Sage, by what means does one come to possess skillful movement and wisdom? [12–13]
One who is free from deceit attains mindfulness; one who is wise and reflects upon the meaning becomes possessed of intelligence.
Furthermore, by guarding the Dharma, the learned and respectful person becomes one who possesses the higher destinies.
By what action is one born in the presence of the Protectors of the World?
The confident Bodhisattva asks her about the meanings of those questions;
because he never creates an obstacle to the gift of Dharma,
he quickly attains a meeting with the Lords of the World.
By what does one avoid the inopportune states (*akṣaṇa*), and by what does one go to a happy rebirth (*sugati*)?
By what does one become heedful (*apramatta*) wherever one is born?
[17] One who is faithful avoids the inopportune states; one who possesses ethical discipline goes to a happy rebirth.

One should constantly cultivate emptiness, remaining vigilant and acting according to the prescribed method. By what means does the purification of karma occur? How is one not bound by the snares of Māra?
And how does a bodhisattva become free from the ruin of the Dharma? [18–19]
Through resolute conviction comes the purification of karma; through vigor comes the subduing of Māra.
One who acts as they speak avoids the ruin of the Dharma. By what means does one come to possess a Brahma-voice and a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird?
O Sage, how do you satisfy sentient beings of diverse inclinations?
With a Brahma-voice, through truthful speech, and with a voice free from harshness, you satisfy those of various dispositions; even when divided, that which is indivisible satisfies them all.
"How does one become long-lived and free from illness?
How does one come to have an invincible retinue, O Great Sage?
One becomes non-violent, long-lived, and free from illness through the practice of non-harming."
And one has an inseparable retinue because of not being divided even from those who are divided.
By what are objects prospered? By what is one not deprived of enjoyments? By what does one become renowned as a great lord wherever one is reborn? [24–25]

Success in wealth comes through non-greed; success in enjoyments through non-envy; great lordship through non-jealousy; and one who is always foremost through being free from pride. How does the divine eye arise, and likewise the divine ear?
And by what means, O Leader, do you know the arising of the thought of enlightenment in sentient beings?
[27] One obtains the eye through a lamp, and the ear is purified by music; through the knowledge of the arising of the thought of enlightenment, their emergence occurs in this way. [28]
By what does one obtain supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and the recollection of former births?
And by what, O Leader, do the outflows (*āsrava*) of the Bodhisattvas come to an end?
[29] Supernatural power comes from the gift of vehicles; recollection comes from the practice of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Avoiding both extremes, he touches the exhaustion of the out-flows (āsrava-kṣaya).
By what action does the inclusion of all dharmas arise?
And how, O Leader, does one become beloved by all sentient beings? [30–31]
One should direct the mind toward awakening for the sake of liberating all sentient beings;
this is the summary of all dharmas, and by means of it, one becomes beloved.
Having trained in what kind of training, and having cultivated what kind of mind?
An omniscient teacher is born who is just like the Sage.
For one should always maintain an even mind toward all sentient beings;
having cultivated an even mind, one becomes a Conqueror who surpasses all.
By what means does one not abandon the thought of awakening throughout all births—
even while in the midst of a dream, let alone when awake?
In whichever villages, regions, or inhabited cities one may dwell—
One encourages others toward awakening; therefore, one does not abandon the thought of enlightenment.
By what means would one possess great strength, always arisen with steadfast power, and remain invincible against millions of Māras wherever one is reborn? [36–37]

Having bestowed here the five essentials as well as fearlessness upon those who are afraid, one will become possessed of great strength, always arisen through that power; and wherever one is reborn, one will be invincible to millions of Māras. [38]
By what is there the perfection of the field? By what is there the perfection of the Saṅgha?
By what is there the perfection of radiance, by which the directions are illuminated?
[39] The perfection of the field is through aspiration; the perfection of the Saṅgha is through gathering.
Having offered a canopy of jewels, the quarters were illuminated by it.
Upon hearing such a prophecy concerning the conduct of the Bodhisattvas in the presence of the Lord of the World, that prince was filled with joy.
Together with those companions, Siṃha spoke these words with palms joined:
"O Sage, we shall train ourselves in this practice that has been prescribed.
Then the Buddha manifested a smile that illuminated many realms.
Ajita asked the Buddha, "O Lord, why have you smiled?
Being thus questioned, the Perfectly Awakened One spoke to Ajita: "Ajita, listen to me as to the purpose for which I smiled here."
Eighty crores and twelve million Buddhas—
all of them were honored by him in the past for the sake of awakening.
Having served the great seer Dīpaṃkara, the supreme among bipeds, [he attained his goal].
When these have been ripened by me and become bestowers of accomplishment,
even in the future, these sixty crores of great seers,
having worshipped Maitreya and the others, will become leaders.
Indeed, there will be a most beautiful aeon named Mahāprabhāsa;
in that single aeon, these supreme among bipeds will appear, and they shall all have one name: Jñānaketudhvaja.
Whatever array belongs to Amitābha, that very same one shall belong to them.
And those who merely hear the names of these bodhisattvas—
for them there shall be no doubt regarding awakening, nor any fear concerning their destiny.
Whoever, having heard this prophecy, shall develop resolute faith,
there is no merit equal to theirs to be found in the three worlds. [51] He who, for hundreds of millions of eons, throughout thousands of Buddha-fields...
Having filled [the world] with jewels, one gives them to the Buddhas out of a desire for awakening;

yet, compared to the merit previously proclaimed, that which belongs to one who, having heard the true Dharma, places faith in it for the sake of awakening, does not approach even a fraction or a part of it. [52–53]
The gods rained down flowers and the triple-thousandfold world system trembled;
eighty million beings set out for supreme enlightenment.
Having attained the five superknowledges, Siṃha, together with the sons of the merchant, [proceeded].
Having fully honored the Buddha for seven days, they were all ordained;
in an instant, they all attained the meditative absorptions and the dhāraṇīs,
fulfilling their purpose for the sake of sentient beings by manifesting the qualities of a Buddha.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the joyful lion, the son of the king.
All the worlds, including the realm of the gods, rejoiced in the words of the Sage.
[57] The *Siṃhaparipṛcchā-mahāyāna-sūtra*, the fourteenth, is completed.
